q: The three broad types of clustering are bottom-up, assignment-based, and top-down. Spectral clustering is:
e: Top-down: find the best cut into two pieces, then recurse. HAC is bottom-up. k-means and k-center are assignment-based.

q: The normalized cut is NCut(S,T) = ?
e: Dividing by volume stops S or T from being too small. The cut on top forces a large split.

q: In the L10 example, why isn't S′ = {h} (a single leaf vertex) the best cut even though its Cut is just 1?
a: Its tiny volume makes NCut large
w: h has no edges at all
A single vertex can't be a cluster
e: Its tiny volume makes NCut large (1.1) vs. 0.367 for S = {a,b,c,d}. Normalization penalizes lopsided cuts.

q: The (unnormalized) graph Laplacian is L₀ = ?
e: D − A (degree matrix minus adjacency matrix). Each row and column sums to 0, like water: as much flows in (D) as flows out (A).

q: The first (smallest) eigenvalue of a graph Laplacian is always:
e: The corresponding eigenvector is constant (e.g., 1/√8 for 8 vertices).

q: The second eigenvector of the Laplacian, used to cut the graph, is called the:
e: Split vertices by sign: S = {v : v₂(v) < 0}. You can also try other thresholds along v₂ and keep the best NCut.

q: How can the 2nd and 3rd eigenvectors together be used?
a: Lay out vertices in 2-D and cut by sign quadrants
w: They must be ignored when making the clustering
They are only useful for directed graphs
They are used to count the edges in the graph
e: Lay out vertices in ℝ² and make a 4-way cut by sign quadrants. For layouts, scale each axis by 1/√λᵢ.

q: The normalized Laplacian is L = ?
w: D − A, then divide by n
I − D⁻¹ A D⁻¹ for all edges
e: I − D^(−1/2) A D^(−1/2)  (= D^(−1/2) L₀ D^(−1/2)). It normalizes each edge by the flow in and out of its endpoints' degrees.

q: Why is the normalized Laplacian almost always preferred for spectral clustering?
a: Its 2nd eigenvector relaxes the Normalized Cut
w: It always has smaller entries than L₀ does
It has no eigenvalues that need computing
It's faster to write down and store by hand
e: Its second eigenvector is the optimal continuous relaxation of the Normalized Cut problem. The real cut is binary. The eigenvector solves the relaxed version with continuous values.

q: After embedding vertices with the first few eigenvectors (scaled by 1/√λᵢ), you can:
w: Only cut by the first eigenvector
e: Run any Euclidean clustering, e.g., Lloyd's for k-means. Smaller eigenvalues correspond to more important directions.

q: A common affinity for spectral clustering on data in ℝᵈ is:
e: σ sets what 'close' means (beyond about 2σ is 'far'). Rounding tiny similarities to 0 speeds things up.

q: Spectral embedding with a Gaussian affinity and the UNNORMALIZED Laplacian is called:
e: It's a form of non-linear dimensionality reduction.

q: Is there a definitive rule for choosing k in clustering?
a: No; it trades judgement for assumptions
w: Yes, always use k = √n for n points
Yes, pick the k with the lowest cost
Yes, always use k = 2 and recurse
e: No; clustering is unsupervised, and methods trade human judgement for model assumptions. More automated methods require more assumptions about the clustering and the data.

q: What does the lecture call data with denser regions but no well-defined separation?
e: A 'smear' (like cream cheese on a bagel). Clustering a smear doesn't add much value. Plot first, using dimensionality reduction if d > 2.

q: Why can't you just pick the k with the lowest clustering cost?
a: Cost always drops as k grows
e: Cost always decreases as k increases (reaching 0 at k = n). Every point can be its own center.

q: The 'elbow' in a cost-vs-k plot is where:
a: Cost goes from falling fast to falling slowly
w: Cost finally reaches exactly zero for that k
Cost is at its highest value over all k
Cost stops falling and starts increasing again
e: Cost changes from decreasing rapidly to decreasing slowly. Caveats: it's not always obvious, and nested clusters can create two elbows (either may be fine).

q: In the silhouette score, a(i) and b(i) are:
a: a = avg to own cluster; b = smallest avg to another
w: a = distance to nearest point; b = to farthest point
a = size of the cluster; b = total number of clusters
a = total clustering cost; b = the number k
e: a(i) = avg distance to others in its own cluster; b(i) = smallest avg distance to another cluster. s(i) = (b(i) − a(i)) / max{a(i), b(i)}.

q: Silhouette s(i) lies in what range, and what does s(i) > 0 mean?
a: [−1, 1]; it fits its own cluster better
w: [0, ∞); the point is probably an outlier
e: [−1, 1]; the point is better off in its own cluster than its next-best one. For singleton clusters, s(i) = 0. Choose the k with the highest average silhouette.

q: For which methods might the silhouette score NOT be meaningful?
e: Density-based clustering (DBScan) or single-link HAC. It assumes a k-means-like model of what a good cluster is.

q: The Bayesian Information Criterion for a model with m parameters on n observations is:
e: Choose the k that minimizes BIC.

q: How many parameters does a k-means clustering in ℝᵈ have (for BIC)?
e: kd (each of the k centers has d coordinates). So the penalty kd ln|X| grows linearly with k, while the negative log-likelihood decreases.

q: When each cluster is fit with an isotropic Gaussian, the maximum-likelihood center is:
e: BIC needs a well-defined likelihood. That works for mixtures of Gaussians and k-means ('X-means'), but is hard for spectral or DBScan.
